title: Week 1: A connected world around 1450 — primary-source and geography studio
objectives: Apply and explain a connected world around 1450 — primary-source and geography studio using the specified independent and transfer tasks.
entry_evidence: Place the previous event and this week's date on a timeline; distinguish a primary witness from later background.

steps.instruction:
Around1450, many societies maintained cities, states and exchange networks; no single place was the centre of all world history. An atlas can locate the Mediterranean, Sahara, Indian Ocean and East Asia, but a modern political map does not show their1450 boundaries. Dates and regional labels are tools, not claims that all peoples shared one period.

READ Martin Waldseemueller, world map,1507. Locator: whole map and catalog's creation date. https://www.loc.gov/item/2003626426/
Edition/use note: Library of Congress catalog and enlarged historical map. Historical representation, not modern borders. Reference viewing; no image files packaged.

Adult previews readings for antisemitism, coercion, enslavement, executions, crime, accounts of suicide and religious controversy. For North's final death accounts and Julius Caesar's violent scenes, preview the exact pages/scenes and omit graphic method details from oral reading or use a neutral account of the outcome. No reenactment or personal disclosure. Explain prejudice without reenacting it or asking a learner to defend a group identity. In Merchant, distinguish a character's slur from the tutor's speech; do not require a learner to speak slurs. Omit abusive words aloud, not the fact that the text contains prejudice. For distress, stop and use an adult's neutral synopsis for analysis, marking that as a supported route rather than independent reading of omitted text. Read Everyman's theology historically; faith, character and assent are never scored.

Use the historical map's date, projection and naming conventions; a modern locator grid is not evidence of old borders. Keep original practice data separate from archival findings.
